titleStmt.title: Response Time Analysis for the Abort-and-Restart Event Handlers of the Priority-Based Functional Reactive Programming (P-FRP) Paradigm

analytic.title: Response Time Analysis for the Abort-and-Restart Event Handlers of the Priority-Based Functional Reactive Programming (P-FRP) Paradigm

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Programming microcontrollers is a different paradigm from microprocessor programming. The traditional way to program microcontrollers is to write the program in C or an assembly language, but modern embedded systems are more complex. The Priority-based Functional Reactive Programming (P-FRP) paradigm could make microcontroller programming better. P-FRP makes it possible to treat programs as functions (stateless) and amenable to proofs and type-safety. In this paper, we focus on the abort-and-restart event handler semantics of P-FRP, which is neither a concurrency control policy nor a true scheduling policy. Instead, it is a policy in which the most important task is scheduled first. This paper refines the response time analysis for the abort-and-restart model on single-core systems. *

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Unlike general-purpose machines, real-time embedded systems interact with the physical world every day, where physics (in particular, constraints on timing, size, weight, and power consumption) cannot be ignored. Some of these systems are complex, such as entire robotic assembly lines. Real-time software is also an important component in most defense and civil aerospace systems. Such software has great advantages for automating tasks, but it also carries very serious risks. The software is extremely fragile and a missed deadline could alter the safe operation of any system. Thus, university and industry researchers are working on better tools and methods for embedded systems co-design.

div.head: The P-FRP Paradigm
div.p: The Priority-based Functional Reactive Programming (P-FRP) paradigm [8] aims to improve the programming of embedded controllers, which are typically programmed with C or assembler. P-FRP programs are written as a collection of functions (stateless) grounded in the mathematics of functions and recurrence relations. The P-FRP compiler generates resource-bounded C code that comprises a group of event handlers, where each event handler is responsible for a single interrupt or event source. The semantics of P-FRP requires that each event handler executes atomically. This requirement facilitates reasoning about P-FRP programs and thus is a desirable feature of the language. However, this means that task preemption is an abort action-the lower-priority task is aborted when a higher-priority task arrives. The task is restarted once the higherpriority task completes. By its nature, P-FRP, with its abort-andrestart scheme, eliminates the priority inversion problem 1 .

div.head: Motivation
div.p: The problem we consider in this paper is how to use the standard response time analysis when utilizing the P-FRP model. The difficulty is that it is not clear whether a model is possible at all. An important performance aspect of the P-FRP model is that the abortand-restart scheduling scheme reduces the priority-inversion problem, but makes the reasoning of the overall system correctness more difficult. Based on the analysis, in some cases the number of aborts is limited by the event set attributes or characteristics, so handlers' response times are bounded. In other cases, the number of aborts is high. Nevertheless, a worst-case response time analysis may show that all tasks indeed finish on time. Therefore, the goal is to refine the standard response time analysis while focusing on the abort-andrestart model. Sporadic tasks, by definition, have a minimum interarrival time, thus, the number of preemptions that they can cause is bounded and so is their impact within an abort and restart framework. For periodic tasks there seems to be the problem of how to stop a high-priority task from arriving just in time to cause a lowpriority task to be aborted. The usual model is to determine whether for task k (low priority with quite a few high-priority tasks in the system), there are C k amount of execution time "gaps" in the higher load before deadline D k . With the P-FRP model as is, we must compute the largest guaranteed gap in D k and show that this is larger than C k . This task is much more difficult and possibly NP-hard (more in Section 4.1.). Moreover, there is more overhead with the model since time spent on task execution is wasted; however, there are no rollback and checkpointing costs. Furthermore, the model does reduce the impact of a wrong decision. It implements executions as function evaluations; therefore, there are no "incomplete" function evaluations, as in the case of a task's interruption. The added computational costs could be considered reasonable, given that the model offers far richer composition than traditional schemes [1,14].

div.head: Organization
div.p: In Section 2, we describe the notation and system model used in the paper. In Section 3, we present a review of the existing response time analysis. Section 4 derives the worst-case response time analysis for the abort-and-restart model, while Section 5 validates the effectiveness of the proposed approach through a set of experiments. In the last section, we summarize the key contributions of this paper and provide some perspectives on future work.

div.head: System Model, Notations and Terminology
div.p: This paper proposes an analytic approach similar to that presented in [2,7], but with the traditional preemptive scheduling assumptions replaced by the assumptions of the abort-and-restart model. We consider a real-time system to comprise one distinct class of tasks: event handlers. Events herein are like interrupts in that each event is associated with an event handler routine that must be executed. Events do not have to come strictly from standalone hardware; inputs and requests can also come from practical devices such as pacemakers, robots, and robotic components such as arms, industrial actuators, etc.

For ease of reference, Table 1 below summarizes the notations used throughout this paper. For the purposes of this paper, we will use the terms task and event interchangeably. To simplify the presentation of the topic, we assume discrete scheduling, that is parameters are taken from the integers and preemptions happen at discrete moments in time. Each event τ i is characterized by a quadruple of non-negative integers (r i , C i , T i , D i ) ∈ Ω, where r i is the arrival time, C i is the worst-case execution time, T i is the period of event τ i , and D i is the relative deadline by which event τ i should be completed. According to the current semantics of P-FRP, events do not have deadlines. The assumption is that the same periodic event will not occur before the prior instance finishes. This guarantees that no event is missed when the queue is full. To keep the theory simple, we assume that every event has a soft deadline that is equal to its period. Nevertheless, the analysis for WCRT under RM is applicable without any change to the case of D i < T i .

div.head: The Abort-and-Restart Scheduling Model
div.p: Preemption with the abort-and-restart policy means that the scheduler aborts the execution of a low-priority event upon the arrival of a high-priority event and immediately executes the high-priority event. This concept of restarts is often used in communication systems where packet transmission is non-preemptive. As soon as all high-priority packets are transmitted, transmission of the aborted low-priority packet restarts from the beginning of the packet. Preemption with resume service policy is similar, except that the preempted low-priority packet resumes from the point of preemption rather than the beginning.

The choice of the appropriate service policy to employ depends on the characteristics of the communication link, the timing requirements of the high-priority packets, and the size of the low-priority packets. If the transmission rate of the communication link is high enough compared to the length and size of the longest low-priority packets, then the delay incurred by a high-priority packet blocked by a low-priority one could be acceptable. In this case, the nopreemption service policy may be preferable because it is easier to implement and may have lower link overhead. If the performance efficiency of the communication link is not important, but the delay associated with the blocking is very high, then the preemption with the abort-and-restart service policy may be acceptable.

With the abort-and-restart service technique of P-FRP, a lowpriority event cannot block a high-priority one. There is always an immediate switch to the high-priority event. Furthermore, events that finish without preemptions can only affect the program state. Shared data is read into scratch variables at the beginning of the event handler's execution. A restoration from the scratch variables at the end of the handler is performed while interrupts are turned off. Furthermore, on a single processor system, neither logging nor validation is required. Thus, if the computation part of an event handler is interrupted, values in the temporary scratch variables are simply discarded. A handler does not affect the program state until the restoration. Therefore, there are no rollback or checkpointing costs where data is shared. Thus, when an event handler is aborted, shared data is already in a stable state and reinitialization is not necessary.

As an example to show how the abort-and-restart model works with RM scheduling, consider the task set A given in Table 2. The abort-and restart approach is not the best answer for every task set. As shown in Figure 1, the behavior of Task1 illustrates the problem. Neither Task2 nor Task3 can complete. Task2 is preempted and aborts as soon as Task1 arrives. Moreover, Task3 cannot run at all. If there is at least one pair of tasks j and i, where task τ j has a higher-priority than task τ i , such that T j -C j < C i , then the task set cannot be scheduled. In this case, there is not a C i amount of free scheduling gap to execute task τ i completely. Thus, task τ i aborts each time task τ j arrives. Accordingly, the abort-and-restart problem is not a simple extension of the standard worst-case response time analysis.
Figure 1. The abort-and-restart strategy with RM scheduling.

div.head: Busy and Idle Periods
div.p: Busy periods are fundamental to the analysis of fixed priority preemptive scheduling. A level-i idle period is defined as a point in time, t, in which there are no tasks of priority i or higher awaiting execution and ready to execute strictly before t. A level-i busy period or deadline busy period (for EDF) is a point in time, t, in which tasks of priority i or higher are processed throughout [a,b]. In the remainder of the paper, references to a busy period refer to the worstcase response.

div.head: Atomicity and Program Correctness
div.p: Concurrent tasks create many problems that did not exist in the purely sequential program. For instance, it is easy for groups of concurrent tasks to interfere with one other. It is imperative that tasks see a consistent system state. Each group of tasks is required to execute their joint activity as indivisible or atomic actions. Of course, a single task may also want to protect itself from the interference of other tasks. Atomicity and the abort-and-restart model make it possible to design flexible stateless events. P-FRP takes the stateless paradigm much further. P-FRP makes it possible to treat programs as functions (stateless) and amenable to proofs and type-safety. P-FRP's close approximation to mathematical functions provides a more direct vehicle for formal proofof-program correctness. In contrast to the imperative style, program state and assignment are absent. There is no need to write triples to keep track of the state transformations as we would with imperative languages. Instead, with P-FRP, we write programs as collections of functions, which allows us to base correctness proofs for P-FRP programs on well-known rules of mathematical induction rather than direct proofs that rely on reasoning about state transformations at each step (i.e., computation step). In general, the verification of P-FRP programs is a much more straightforward process than the verification of imperative programs.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: Rate Monotonic Analysis (RMA) was introduced by Liu and Layland in 1973 [9]. Their work presented a test to see if a real-time system could be guaranteed to meet its deadlines. The test was limited in the range of the systems it could address and it assumed that all tasks in the system were periodic, had deadlines at the end of their periods, and were independent of one another. Further work on scheduling tests lifted many of the earlier restrictions where tasks access shared resources, as in Baker's Stack Resource Policy (SRP) [3] and Sha et al's Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) [14]. Joseph and Pandya [7] introduced scheduling tests based on finding the worstcase response time of each task. Audsley et al [2], Spuri [15], and Tindell [17] later extended the tests.

The idea of abort-and-restart is not new: it has been a fundamental part of database design and synchronization policies for many years. Takada and Sakamura [16] presented a real-time synchronization protocol enabling the ability to abort critical sections. This technique divides a critical section into two segments and assigns a priority ceiling to each. Tasks that have a higher priority than the priority ceiling of the currently executed segment can abort the critical section. When necessary, executed critical sections inherit the priority of the blocked task; however, priority inheritance protocols have notable disadvantages. For example, inheritance algorithms are complicated and easy to get wrong. Many more disadvantages are described in [18]. Vitek et al [11] present a concurrencycontrol abstraction for real-time Java called Preemptible Atomic Region (PAR), which is very similar to the transaction mechanism. PAR is a sequence of instructions guaranteed to execute atomically. If a higher-priority task is released, the PAR is rolled back and the higher-priority task executes as if the lower-priority task never ran. Once the lower-priority task is rescheduled, the PAR restarts. Ringenburg et al [13] present software transactions (STMs) based on atomicity and rollback. An STM prohibits interleaved computation in atomic blocks while ensuring fairness (as defined by Grossman in [6]). An atomic block must run as though no other thread runs in parallel and must eventually commit its computation results. Ringenburg et al uses logging and rollback to abort uncompleted atomic blocks upon thread preemption and retry them when the thread is rescheduled.

div.head: The Response Time Analysis Problem
div.p: The most important property of a real-time system is the fulfillment of timing constraints [5]. Fast execution speeds could help meet stringent timing constraints, but fast execution alone cannot guarantee the fulfillment of timing constraints. Although some classes of real-time systems with predictable response times do exist, the amount of time required to predict their response time is usually large. Selecting a language that is suitable for programming hard real-time systems can dramatically reduce the time needed to analyze these systems.

div.head: RTA for Fixed-Priority Scheduling (FPS)
div.p: In fixed priority (FP) scheduling, tasks are statically assigned fixed priories. Response time analysis is applicable to any fixed priority scheduling algorithm. The approach taken by response time analysis is as follows:
1. Determine the worst-case pattern that leads to the worst-case response time for task τ i .
2. Compute worst-case response time for task τ i .
3. Determine the task's ability to be scheduled by determining whether task τ i meets its deadline.

For synchronous systems, Tindell et al [17] said that the worstcase response time for task τ i occurs following a critical instant where task τ i is released simultaneously with all higher-priority tasks, and all tasks are subject to their maximum release jitter 4 . However, the critical instant argument may not apply completely to our model. If the critical instance is hard to find then this usually means that the problem is going to be intractable. Accordingly, we use pessimistic worst-case execution times. Therefore, the worst case is never underestimated. Thus, for the highest-priority task, its worstcase response time will equal its own execution time (that is, WCRT = C). However, other tasks will suffer interference from higherpriority tasks, because of the time spent executing higher-priority tasks when a lower-priority task is ready to run.

div.head: Blocking and Interference Costs
div.p: To analyze the interactions among tasks executing on a singlecore platform, we must define the two parameters of blocking and inter f erence.

Interference I i (a, b) on a task τ i over an interval [a, b] is the cumulative length of all intervals in which task τ i is ready to run, but where the processor is executing higher-priority tasks. For a general task τ i :
div.formula: WCRT i = C i + B int + I i . (1
div.p: where B int is the worst-case blocking time. Event arrivals are blocked while interrupts are disabled to update critical shared data. I i is the maximum interference from higher-priority tasks that a task can experience in any interval [t,t + WCRT i ). As stated previously, the maximum interference occurs when all higher-priority tasks are released at the same time as task τ i (that is, at a critical instant). Without loss of generality, we can assume that all tasks release at time 0. Within the interval, [0,WCRT i ), a higher-priority task τ j will be released a number of times. Each release of task τ j imposes an interference of C j on task τ i . We can now modify Equation (1) to account for this number of releases:
div.formula: WCRT i = C i + B int + ∑ ∀ j∈hp i WCRT i T j •C j .(2)

div.head: Abort-and-Restart Costs
div.p: In the P-FRP paradigm, if a higher-priority task (i.e., urgent) comes in while the machine is busy, then the task does not have to wait until the current job is finished. We could abort the processing of the current job and start the new, urgent one. This is the same as applying preemption, but with one major difference: In the case of preemption, the job can continue at the place where it was interrupted; that is, the time already spent on the job is subtracted from its processing time. In the case of restart, the job must start the processing all over again. The time spent on a job where the processing is broken off is wasted and recorded as lost time. But allowing restarts reduces the impact of a wrong decision, which means that there are no incomplete function evaluations, as in the case of an interrupted task. Therefore, the use of the abort-and-restart scheme does introduce some costs, which can be computed as follows:
div.formula: α i = N ∑ j=i+1 WCRT i T j • j-1 max k=i C k . (3
div.p: α i is the maximum computation time that could be lost because of aborts-and-restarts. Here, C k is the maximum worst-case execution time that results from preempting then aborting the task. The equation assumes that the worst-case execution time aborted will be from task τ i or a higher-priority task that is between task τ i and the highest-priority task.

Theorem 1 (WCRT for abort-and-restart with FP). An upper bound on the response time of a task τ i in a FP-scheduled uniprocessor system using the abort-and-restart scheme can be derived by the fixed-point iteration on the value w m+1 of the following expression, starting with an initial w 0 i = C i :
div.formula: WCRT i = w m+1 i + α i . (4
w m+1 i = C i + B int + ∑ ∀ j∈hp i w m i T j •C j .
div.p: Proof. Consider the point for release of task τ i . We need to show both of the following:
1. The case where there is no interference: We want to determine whether the equation computes the correct result when there is no interference and blocking.
2. The interference case: Assuming that the equation computes the correct result for the no interference case, we want to compute the case with interference.

The no interference case is the simplest step -all the tasks are linear, and there is no interference from higher-priority tasks, thus there are no aborts-and-restarts. For example, if task A has the highest priority, it must be executed before task B, and task B must run before task τ i , and so on (Figure 2). In this simple example, at time 0, (the notional release time of task τ i ), we assume all higher-priority tasks were released. Thus, the worst-case bound for the WCRT i can be computed as follows:
div.formula: w 1 i = C i + ∑ ∀ j∈hp i C j(5)
div.p: Therefore, Equation 5 handles the case when there is no interference. It is simply the sum of all execution times. Furthermore, there is no blocking since tasks execute in a fixed-priority order.

For the interference case, we assume that higher-priority tasks will re-arrive and preempt task τ i . From the point of release of task τ i until the task completes, the processor will be in a P i -busy period-the processor will execute tasks with priority P i or higher. However, computation at the P i level cannot begin until the computations for all higher-priority levels are complete. Consider w i to be a time window that moves down the level-i busy period. At time 0, we assume that task τ i and all higher-priority tasks have been released. This would be the end of the busy period unless task τ i completes before it suffers interference and aborts. If one or more higher-priority tasks arrive before task τ i completes, then the computation window will need to increase because it will take longer to execute these tasks and re-execute task τ i . The window will continue to expand as demand increases. If computational demand does not increase, then the busy period is done. The width of the window is the response time of task τ i . If the window continues to expand, the equation would never converge and wmi would never equal w m+1 i , meaning that the demand is greater than the available processor time. In this case, Equation (4) has no solution, and we can assume the task set cannot be scheduled. This completes the proof.

div.head: Abort-and-Restart with EDF
div.p: Some researchers may argue that computing response times under EDF scheduling may not be necessary. We could just derive inflated worst-case execution times for event handlers that include the times required for retries, and then use EDF's well-known utilization bound test [9]. Although this is another way to approach the problem, we still need to know the number of retries, and finding this is a key problem. We cannot simply use existing analysis that assumes either preemptive or non-preemptive task models.

One of the disadvantages of using the EDF scheduling algorithm is that each task's worst-case response time may not happen when all tasks are released at a critical instant. In the critical instant situation, only tasks with a shorter relative deadline will interfere with task τ i . However, at a later point, some or all tasks may have a shorter absolute deadline than task τ i . For example, consider a three-task system as depicted in Table 3 andFigure Upon rearriving at t = 10, task τ C is still active and has a shorter deadline (16 versus 20). Therefore, task τ C takes precedence. Accordingly, task τ A has a response time of 3, which is three times the value obtained at time 0, a critical instant. Later releases may give larger values, but they are bounded at 10 because the system can be scheduled by EDF (total processor utilization .85). Thus, the EDF scheduling scheme is more complex for computing worst-case response times. All task releases must be considered in order to see which releases suffer the most interference and the most aborts from tasks with shorter absolute deadlines.

Although more releases must be considered, computing the worstcase response time can be done in a way similar to RM scheduling. The worst-case response time of τ i s instance, released at time t=y, can be found by computing the length of the busy period of all tasks preceding τ i s instance that have deadlines less than or equal to task τ i s deadline [15]. If we let L i (y) be the length of the busy period relative to the deadline d = y + D i , then for any general task τ i , the formula to compute the worst-case response time is as follows:
div.formula: WCRT i (y) = max y≥0 {C i , L i (y) + B int + α i -y}(6)
div.p: Since we are certain that C i is a lower bound for any task τ i s , we must check if the upper bound is greater than C i . The computation of L i (y) is found by a recursive method similar to that given for RM scheduling.

div.head: Case Study
div.p: In order to evaluate the analysis, we ran simulations with functional reactive programming to assess the performance of the abortand-restart scheme of P-FRP under RM and EDF scheduling. We used the theory of the GAP (Generic Avionics Platform) task set. GAP is a case study of an avionics mission computer system model that was created by Locke et al [10]. GAP models the aircraft computer system's functionality and data handling constraints. Some of the avionics timing constraints are:

1. Navigation: 20 Hz repetition, based on accuracy requirements. Of the seventeen tasks in the GAP set, all but one task are strictly periodic. The exception, Task 11, is a sporadic task. In our experiments we assume all tasks are strictly periodic and do not suffer any release jitter . Although the abort-and-restart scheme of P-FRP is not a resource access protocol, its performance with reference to SRP or PCP may still be of interest. PCP and SRP are obviously more efficient since time spent on a task execution is never wasted. Thus, the motivation for the comparison can be to observe how much is the penalty introduced by abort-and-restart. The conclusion should be that the penalty is negligible for the faster tasks but grows for slower tasks (if tasks are sorted by growing periods).

We structured the task set to have priority inversions without a protocol, since there will be task sets that make one protocol appear more effective and vice versa. We also ran a variety of tests to find out what makes one protocol more suitable than the other. The results of the worst-case response times are in Figures 5 to 8. The graphs show the results of analyses of the same task set using both the static Rate Monotonic (RM) scheduling algorithm and the dynamic Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling algorithm.

The first and second experiments used RM scheduling. From the first graph, we can make several observations. Note that the performance of RM depends on the arrival pattern; in the worst case, tasks arrive at the same time and present a maximum disadvantage for lower-priority tasks. Figure 5 shows that both the SRP and the PCP performed similarly, with the PCP doing slightly better. As expected, the response time estimates obtained from the non-preemptive analysis are shorter than those obtained from the abort-and-restart strategy. Since re-execution costs are higher, the abort-and-restart technique did not perform well. On the other hand, the non-preemptive analysis did not perform much better. Some high-priority tasks missed their deadlines because the waiting times were longer. On the other side, there are more missed deadlines with SRP than PCP caused by the additional blocking with the SRP. The PCP adheres to the priority-scheduling model better since the priority of a task is only raised when necessary [11]. In the second experiment, we focused on the number and length of each critical section. The test showed that with fewer and shorter critical sections, SRP performed better than before. Looking at Figure 6 it is apparent that both the SRP and the PCP are almost equal. SRP's performance improved when the number of critical sections was reduced by half and their lengths were shortened. Priority inheritance means there is potentially higher overhead. Even so, the abort-and-restart strategy did not deliver good performance. At the other extreme, when the tasks are non-preemptive, we see that even with shorter and lighter resources the task set is not able to be scheduled due to increased waiting times.

The third experiment shows that the performance is far better with EDF scheduling than with RM. In Figure 7, the results of EDF scheduling and heavy resource usage indicate that the response time estimates from the non-preemptive analysis are shorter than those obtained from the abort-and-restart model. However, the abort-andrestart scheme performed well. Under EDF scheduling, there is less interference from higher-priority tasks, because tasks with a shorter absolute deadline have a higher priority. SRP performed much better with EDF than with RM scheduling. However, the performance of PCP was better than the rest -the worst-case response times of all tasks were lower than that of the other tests. The results of the abort-and-restart strategy and also the nonpreemptive analysis are very good. Figure 8 displays the results of the experiments with EDF scheduling and lighter and shorter critical sections (the number of critical sections was reduced by a half). As one should expect and we noted in previous experiments [12] PCP performs better for a higher percentage of resource usage. The performances of SRP and PCP are essentially the same, with PCP performing slightly better. PCP's better performance is due to its adherence to priority scheduling. Priority change is simpler than context switching when implemented over kernel-based threads. Normal OS processes involve a trap into the kernel and a return. It is a similar operation to a thread context switch but still less complex than a process switch (since the memory mapping is not changed).

Finally and most importantly note that saying that abort-and-restart performs very badly under RM and very well under EDF is not 100% accurate. The ratio between the WCRT under abort-and-restart and PCP/SRP is approximately the same under EDF and RM. However, all WCRTs under EDF are shorter, thus all tasks meet their deadlines. Note that the EDF figures have smoother curves because all tasks with the same relative deadline have the same WCRT. Tasks with the same deadline can execute in any order. The worst case for each task is when it runs last in the group with the same deadline, so each task has the same worst-case response time.

div.head: A Case Study in Hardware Implementation
div.p: We thought it would be much more interesting to present a case study that is more than a simple scheduling exercise. To evaluate the performance of P-FRP further, we also present a real hardware experimentation. Because of time and budget constraints-our research and tuition are paid for with our own limited financial resources-it would be difficult to build industrial-size projects. Nevertheless, the control principles that we implemented and tested are very similar to industrial applications that control a Mars Rover or even a Missile Seeker System as shown in Figure 9. The hardware board used to evaluate the algorithms was designed and built around a standard 8-bit microcontroller running P-FRPcompiled code. We used Analog Devices' ADuC814 microcontroller. The microcontroller core is the 8052 and is compatible with Intel's 8051 instruction set. Figure 10 The firmware code and the experiments (real-time task sets) were compiled into 8052-compatible machine language. The files generated were then stored in the processor's memory. These files are programmed into the internal Flash memory of the microcontroller using the built-in bootloader function, which waits for the appropriate sequence on the serial input, receives the serial input, and writes it to the internal Flash program space memory. The bootloader executes when the microcontroller powers up with a special pin active; otherwise, the microcontroller runs the program in memory. Once the microcontroller is reset in run mode, the instructions programmed in memory are read and executed by the microcontroller. Resetting the microcontroller is the same as powering it up. External Flash memory is also connected to the microcontroller, which is accessed via the Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI). The memory device can be read at any address, and has a self-programming cycle that writes 256-byte pages.

Once programmed with the code and algorithms, and upon receiving input from any sensor, the microcontroller executes one of the real-time test experiments. The typical output of an experiment is first stored in memory and then transferred to a desktop computer for analysis.

It is commonly believed that EDF scheduling introduces a larger runtime overhead than RM scheduling, since with EDF absolute deadlines need to be updated from one job to the next, thereby slightly increasing the time needed to execute a job. However, with RM scheduling, a task's priority is based on its period so the overhead is less. In spite of the extra computation time to update absolute deadlines when employing EDF, the live microcontroller tests with tasks having random integer periods showed that EDF had far less runtime overhead, especially when aborts and context switches are taken into account. Figure 11 shows the average number of aborts introduced by RM and EDF. Fixed-priority ordering caused the number of aborts to be always higher under RM scheduling. Although the results show no significant difference to past preemptive scheduling tests [4], the results still illustrate the behavior of RM and EDF with the abort-and-restart model. For small task sets, the number of aborts is more likely to increase. However, as the number of tasks in the system gets higher, in general, worst-case execution times get smaller. This keeps the total processor utilization constant, so the chance for a task to be aborted is reduced. As evident from the previous experiment, such a reduction is much more significant under EDF.

In another experiment, we tested the behavior of EDF and RM for a fixed number of tasks as a function of the CPU load. Figure 12 shows the average number of abortions as a function of the load for a set of 10 periodic tasks with an average load ranging from .5 to 0.95. It is interesting to observe the different behavior of EDF and RM for high-processor loads. For example, under EDF, increasing execution times do not always mean a higher number of aborts, because a task with a long period could still have an absolute deadline shorter than that of a task with shorter period. Under RM, however, the number of aborts increases with the load, because tasks with longer execution times have a greater chance of being aborted by tasks with higher priorities.

The easiest way to measure the difference in processor loading is to measure the current draw of the chip. This can be done with a simple meter. We conducted many experiments to test the hypothesis, but we found no difference between one algorithm and another. Figure 13 shows the current flowing into the ADuC814 microcontroller while running the abort-and-restart under RM and EDF. The Y-axis is the current used by the ADuC814 chip. The X-axis is time. The voltage is 3.3V, so the power dissipated is (P = 3.3V x I). The ADuC814 microcontroller uses the same amount of current regardless what algorithm it is running. The moving average plots filter out the high-frequency 'noise'. Each point on the graph is the average of the previous 25 samples.

div.head: Conclusions and Future Work
div.p: This paper evaluates a real-time policy for running tasks called abort-and-restart. We show a new method for analyzing the ability to schedule task sets under the abort-and-restart model. We tested the performance of the model using simulations and on an 8052 (ADuC814 Analog Devices) microcontroller-driven hardware platform running our compiled test code. The problem was examined under rate monotonic (RM) and earliest deadline first (EDF) scheduling. The results show that when EDF scheduling is used, abort-andrestart is more effective than when using the RM algorithm. The disadvantages of using a non-mainstream policy such as the abort-andrestart scheme may outweigh the advantages in some projects. For example, with aborts-and-restarts more overhead is incurred when tasks abort and the execution time is lost. However, allowing restarts reduces the impact of a wrong decision. Abort-and-restart implements executions as function evaluations. There are no "incomplete" function evaluations, as when a task is interrupted. The model does provide a substrate for real-time programming that offers richer composition than has been available to date. Therefore, we propose that future work apply a similar analytical approach to multi-core systems. However, early results show that disabling interrupts before updating a critical region will not work on multi-core systems.
